rv.q: The Honey Trap comes together with devastating force in its final moments.
McGann compassionately tells all perspectives on the story as participants on every side of this deadly triangle reveal the pain and anguish their people have endured.
Without giving anything away, I’ll say that The Honey Trap is one of the most riveting psychological thrillers I’ve seen onstage in some time.
This is one of the strongest new plays Irish Rep has offered in a good long while.

A taut psychological thriller dedicated to the proposition that, at some point in an endless cycle of revenge, root causes cease to matter, The Honey Trap hinges on two distinct games of cat and mouse.
Belfast playwright Leo McGann’s new drama amalgamates an odd blend of genres; but as supported by very good acting and staging, Irish Rep’s premiere delivers an undeniably entertaining two hours.

Though The Honey Trap clamps down in an emotionally stunning conclusion, a reviewer’s mild query is whether in the Dave/Charlie twist does McGann risk confusing literally inclined spectators too much before revealing his devastating destination?
But this play picks a narrower path and we end up watching Dave stage his own personal skin-crawling honey trap which frustratingly did not illuminate much beyond his rage.

Returning to the same stage it first occupied last fall, The Honey Trap remains a profoundly captivating unraveling, one that seeps into the bloodstream, quickening the pulse, and tightening the chest as it hurtles toward an inexorable climax.
What makes Caroline compelling as a play is that its core problem is universal, not issue-specific.
Matt Torney’s beautiful direction choices boldly demand an accountability that is later posited to be impossible.

“The Honey Trap” offers no catharsis, no closure, no hope that understanding the past can free us from it. It’s a play that lingers like guilt itself—uncomfortable, inescapable, and impossible to resolve.
The Honey Trap is another prize, another winner, on Irish Repertory Theatre’s shelf of good historical dramas with deep psychological underpinnings that make for a great night out at the theatre.
McGann ramps up the tension to an ending that is both shockingly unexpected and yet feels absolutely right.
With a strong ensemble and a script that refuses easy answers, this production offers audiences both a gripping story and a sobering reminder of how the past continues to shadow the present.
The Honey Trap is a gripping thriller that explores the Troubles in a unique and compelling way.

cn.t: McGann's gripping thriller about The Troubles earns strong praise for its intricate structure and Michael Hayden's volcanic lead performance, though some critics find the plot twists implausible and complex subjects oversimplified.

vr.q: I thought the theatre was lovely and better yet, so was the play.
This was just a top rate production. I really enjoyed it.
